prompt: You must check whether any value appears more than once in an unsorted list of a million numbers. Which approach fits best?
choices: Compare every pair with nested loops
Hash Set membership check while scanning
explanation: A hash set answers 'have I seen this?' in O(1), so one scan is O(n) time, O(n) space. Nested loops are O(n^2), and binary search needs sorted data.

prompt: Given two words, decide whether one is an anagram of the other (same letters, rearranged).
explanation: Count each letter in one word, subtract with the other: O(n) time, O(1) space for a fixed alphabet. Permutations are factorial — hopeless past a few letters.

prompt: Find two numbers in a SORTED array that add up to a target, using constant extra space.
choices: Hash map of values already seen
Two pointers moving inward from both ends
explanation: Because the array is sorted, a too-small sum means advance the left pointer, too-big means retreat the right: O(n) time, O(1) space. A hash map also works but costs O(n) space.

prompt: Check whether a phrase reads the same forwards and backwards, ignoring spaces and punctuation.
choices: Two pointers moving toward the middle
Binary search for the middle character
explanation: Walk one pointer from each end, skipping non-letters, comparing as you go: O(n) time, O(1) space — no reversed copy needed.

prompt: Find the length of the longest substring that contains no repeated characters.
choices: Sliding window with a set of characters inside it
explanation: Grow the window right; on a repeat, shrink from the left until it's gone. Each character enters and leaves at most once: O(n) time, O(k) space. Checking all substrings is O(n^2) or worse.

prompt: Compute the maximum sum of any contiguous run of exactly k elements in an array.
choices: Fixed-size sliding window: add the entering element, subtract the leaving one
Merge sort, then take the top k
Recompute each window's sum from scratch
explanation: Each slide updates the sum in O(1), so the whole pass is O(n) time, O(1) space. Recomputing every window costs O(n*k).

prompt: Verify that the brackets ( ) [ ] { } in a code file are balanced and properly nested.
choices: Push opens on a stack; each close must match the top
explanation: A stack remembers the most recent unclosed bracket, catching bad nesting like ( [ ) ] that a simple counter misses: O(n) time, O(n) space.

prompt: For each day's temperature, find how many days you must wait for a warmer one.
choices: Monotonic decreasing stack of unresolved days
Hash map from temperature to day
explanation: Keep a stack of days still waiting; each new day pops every colder day and resolves it. Every index is pushed and popped once: O(n) time, O(n) space.

prompt: Find a target value in a sorted array that was rotated at some unknown pivot (like [4,5,6,1,2,3]).
choices: Modified binary search: recurse into whichever half is sorted
explanation: One half of any split is always properly sorted, so you can decide which half may hold the target: O(log n) time, O(1) space, versus O(n) for a scan.

prompt: Detect whether a linked list loops back on itself, using O(1) memory.
choices: Fast and slow pointers (tortoise and hare)
explanation: A pointer moving two steps laps a pointer moving one step if and only if there's a cycle: O(n) time, O(1) space. The hash set works but uses O(n) memory.

prompt: Reverse a singly linked list in place.
choices: Iterate with prev/curr pointers, flipping each next link
Copy values to an array, reverse it, rebuild the list
Swap the first and last values repeatedly via full scans
explanation: One walk flipping next pointers as you go: O(n) time, O(1) space. Copying to an array works but doubles the memory and misses the point of the structure.

prompt: Compute the maximum depth (longest root-to-leaf path) of a binary tree.
explanation: Each node's depth is one more than its deeper child — a natural recursion visiting every node once: O(n) time, O(h) space for the call stack.

prompt: Build an autocomplete: given a typed prefix, quickly return all stored words that start with it.
choices: Trie (prefix tree), walk the prefix then collect the subtree
Hash map keyed by full word
Unsorted array with a linear scan per keystroke
explanation: A trie shares prefixes structurally, so reaching all matches costs O(prefix length) plus output size. A hash map only answers exact-word lookups — it can't enumerate by prefix.

prompt: Tasks with priorities stream in continuously; you must always process the highest-priority one next.
choices: Re-sort the whole list after every arrival
Hash map from priority to task
explanation: A heap inserts and extracts the max in O(log n) each. Re-sorting on every arrival costs O(n log n) per task, and a FIFO queue ignores priority entirely.

prompt: Generate every possible subset of a set of 10 distinct items.
choices: Backtracking: at each item, branch on include vs. exclude
Greedily pick the largest items first
explanation: The include/exclude decision tree enumerates all 2^n subsets exactly once: O(2^n * n) time — unavoidable, since the output itself has 2^n entries.

prompt: Find the shortest path between two rooms in a maze where every step costs the same.
explanation: BFS explores in rings of increasing distance, so the first time you reach the goal is via a shortest path: O(V+E) time. DFS finds *a* path, not the shortest one.

prompt: Count the distinct ways to climb n stairs when each move is 1 or 2 steps.
explanation: The last move came from step n-1 or n-2, giving a Fibonacci-style recurrence: O(n) time, O(1) space. Enumerating actual sequences is exponential.

prompt: Count the unique paths from the top-left to the bottom-right of a grid, moving only right or down.
explanation: Each cell is reachable only from above or from the left, so its count is the sum of those two: O(rows*cols) time. Storing every path explodes combinatorially.

prompt: Each array index holds a max jump length. Decide whether you can reach the last index from the first.
choices: Greedy: sweep once, tracking the furthest reachable index
explanation: If the furthest-reachable frontier ever falls behind your position, you're stuck; if it reaches the end, you win. One pass: O(n) time, O(1) space.

prompt: Given a list of meeting time ranges, merge every set of overlapping meetings into one block.
choices: Sort by start time, then sweep and merge neighbors
Hash map from start to end times
explanation: Once sorted by start, an interval can only overlap the block being built — extend it or start a new one: O(n log n) for the sort, then a linear sweep.
